query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled isothermal aging treatment that induces nanoscale coherent precipitate formation in a titanium–nickel primary high‐entropy alloy will enhance its high-temperature yield strength and creep resistance compared to the as‐cast alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: An as‐cast high-entropy alloy with titanium and nickel as primary constituents (along with at least three other elements present at 5–35 at% each) produced by vacuum induction melting and homogenized to yield a single-phase matrix.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to an isothermal aging heat treatment at 700°C for 3 hours in an inert (argon) atmosphere, followed by rapid quenching to room temperature.
generation.conditions: After treatment, perform high-temperature mechanical tests (e.g., constant strain rate tensile tests and creep tests) at 800°C under a controlled inert atmosphere.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of nanoscale coherent precipitates (likely intermetallic phases) uniformly distributed within the primary matrix.
generation.mechanism: Precipitation strengthening: the nanoscale precipitates obstruct dislocation motion and delay grain boundary sliding at elevated temperatures, leading to improved yield strength and creep resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in high-temperature yield strength and an improvement in creep resistance (longer creep lifetime or reduced creep rate) relative to the as-cast baseline.
generation.baseline: The same titanium–nickel primary high-entropy alloy produced and tested without the post-solidification heat treatment.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to high-entropy alloys with titanium and nickel as primary elements (with other elements each in the range of 5–35 at%) when operating at elevated temperatures (around 800°C) in inert atmospheres. It is limited to alloys manufactured via melting and homogenized casting routes.
generation.uncertainty: While the mechanism of precipitation strengthening is well established in various alloy systems, the exact precipitate phase, optimal aging parameters, and the precise magnitude of mechanical improvement in this novel composition remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same titanium–nickel primary high-entropy alloy batch. Apply the isothermal aging treatment (700°C for 3 hours in argon, followed by quenching) to one set, while leaving the other set in the as-cast state. Conduct high-temperature tensile tests and creep tests at 800°C. Use transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to verify the presence, size, and distribution of nanoscale precipitates in the aged samples.
measurements: Creep rate and/or creep lifetime under a defined load at 800°C
Microstructural characterization (precipitate size, volume fraction, and distribution via TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aged samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements (e.g., higher yield strength and reduced creep rate or longer creep lifetime) compared to the as-cast samples, or if TEM fails to reveal the expected nanoscale precipitates in the aged microstructure, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.
